abstract: Asparagine contributes to protein function through its polar carboxamide side chain and serves as the acceptor residue for N-linked glycosylation, yet temporally controlling these roles directly through the side-chain carboxamide remains challenging. Here, we report the genetic encoding of N4-(2-nitrobenzyl)-L-asparagine (ONBN), a photocaged asparagine that regenerates the native side-chain carboxamide upon 365 nm irradiation. Engineered aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase/tRNA pairs enabled site-specific ONBN incorporation into proteins in Escherichia coli and mammalian cells. Photodecaging restored Renilla luciferase activity and activated TRAF6 polyubiquitination mediated by UBE2N in living cells. Beyond active-site residues, we further developed CAGE-proxN, using computationally guided proximal caging to optically activate firefly luciferase. Finally, ONBN incorporation at the acceptor position of an N-glycosylation sequon enabled light-triggered initiation and time-resolved monitoring of post-translational glycan installation on an endoplasmic reticulum-targeted reporter. Variation of the -2 flanking residue revealed sequence-dependent differences in apparent glycosylation kinetics. This work extends genetically encoded photocontrol to the asparagine carboxamide and provides a platform for investigating asparagine-dependent protein functions and the temporal regulation of N-glycosylation in living cells.
